newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament increases pressure on premier.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament increases pressure on premier.

text.p: Russia's upper house of parliament, increasing pressure on embattled Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, said on Tuesday the government was not up to the task of tackling the country's problems.

The rebuke by the Federation Council was a deep humiliation for Chernomyrdin, who had just defended his record to the chamber and promised to pay off huge backlogs of wages and debts which have prompted strikes and widespread discontent.
"The government action is inadequate to the situation in the country and society," the Federation Council said in a non-binding resolution addressed to President Boris Yeltsin.
"The Federation Council asks the president to immediately carry out radical measures to provide more efficient work by the government in social-economic development."
The criticism was a new low-point for the 58-year-old prime minister, one of Yeltsin's staunchest allies, in a crisis which has left him increasingly isolated.

Coalminers are on strike across the country, the lower house of parliament is resisting his 1997 spending plans and many public sector workers have staged sporadic protests after not being paid for months.

Problems are also mounting for the Kremlin as Yeltsin, 65, recovers from heart surgery. It has suffered a string of defeats in regional elections and fears isolation on the international stage as NATO prepares to take in members from eastern Europe.
In another blow, the U.S.-based rights monitor Human Rights Watch/Helsinki said Russia's human rights record had not improved this year except for an end to fighting in Chechnya.
Chernomyrdin, who refuses to print money to get out of the crisis and says wage arrears are partly due to widespread tax evasion, defended his economic record and vowed to pay off wage arrears.

"In all main spheres, except the army, 100 percent of debts will be repaid in December. This way we will make our debts disappear and will not allow new indebtedness to form and grow," Chernomyrdin told the Federation Council.

He said the government planned to settle all debts on unpaid pensions and start regular monthly pension payments at the start of next year. But such promises have proved empty in the past and Chernomyrdin did not say where the money would come from.

He also runs a huge risk in not ending the wage arrears to servicemen. The army has no right to go on strike but there have been rumblings of discontent from soldiers, despite Defence Minister Igor Rodionov's assurances there will be no mutiny.
The Federation Council has traditionally been compliant to the demands of Yeltsin and the government, but turned against Chernomyrdin after he refused to address it last week.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was following the situation closely, particularly the miners' strike.
Yastrzhembsky told a Kremlin briefing that Yeltsin, now at the Rus residence west of Moscow, was continuing to make a good recovery from his heart surgery on November 5.
"He is determined to return to work in the Kremlin in the last 10 days of December," Yastrzhembsky said.
